summary:
A visitor to Missouri stands under the national framework of the United States in every setting. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and the Supreme Court allowed those passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation.

Airport screening carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Visa decisions follow the same national rules. In February 2025 the State Department announced that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the marking SWS25, and that listing a gender other than sex assigned at birth can be treated as fraud and a permanent bar. In April 2025 several foreign governments issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules.

Missouri prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023. A transgender visitor under 18 therefore cannot obtain hormones, puberty blockers or transition-related surgery in the state, while those already in treatment are exempted from the hormone and blocker prohibition.

The SAFE Act's reach extends beyond minors. It bars MO HealthNet Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, exposes violating providers to licence revocation, and leaves patients able to sue a provider up to 15 years after treatment. The law sunsets in 2027 as the product of a Republican-Democrat concession, but lawmakers seek to make it permanent and a November 2026 ballot initiative also aims to ban such care indefinitely.

The litigation has not produced relief. A Missouri judge upheld Senate Bill 49 on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the ban on gender-transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar law. Counsel for the plaintiffs, Lambda Legal and the ACLU of Missouri, said they would appeal, and suit continues toward trial on the merits.

Detention in Missouri carries a further care risk. Governor Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations law, effective 2 July 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. The ban took effect without an injunction challenge reported in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
Missouri's care ban sits within a wider national pattern rather than standing alone. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states nationally, and Missouri became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to bar gender-affirming care for inmates. Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical prison-care laws, while similar measures in Idaho and Georgia were blocked by federal courts, so enforcement of such bans depends on jurisdiction.

Federal measures in the same period have been contested. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19; several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court. Missouri's own care ban has survived state and federal challenge to date.

Facilities access is restricted across a growing number of states: a Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia having no such ban, and in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the fourth state to be marked "Do Not Travel" for trans people and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights nationwide.
localsOnly:
Missouri's Senate Bill 49 was filed as suit on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner on behalf of three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA, seeking to block the law before its 28 August 2023 effective date. The court denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023, a Missouri judge upheld the law on 25 November 2024, and the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld it on 13 January 2026; counsel for the plaintiffs announced an appeal, and the case continues toward trial on the merits.

For Missouri residents the practical effects include a prohibition on hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless already in treatment, a prohibition on all transition-related surgeries for minors, loss of MO HealthNet Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care at any age, restricted treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, licence revocation for providers who violate the ban, and patient malpractice claims that may be brought up to 15 years after treatment.

Residents face a closing window rather than a repeal: the SAFE Act sunsets in 2027, lawmakers want the ban made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to ban gender-affirming care for minors indefinitely.

Transgender people held in Missouri prisons lose state-funded cross-sex hormones and gender-transition surgery from 2 July 2026 under an appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe, with no taper plan for those already receiving care.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the appeal announced by Lambda Legal and the ACLU of Missouri after the November 2024 ruling was carried to the U.S. Supreme Court, and whether any petition remains pending after the Missouri Supreme Court's 13 January 2026 decision, is unresolved in the sources.

The sources do not state whether the prison-care funding ban effective 2 July 2026 has been challenged in court, or whether it differs from the Idaho and Georgia measures that federal courts blocked.

No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime penalties, non-discrimination protections, or police conduct toward trans people in Missouri, so those protections are not sourced rather than absent.

Whether an adult trans visitor can obtain a routine refill of hormone therapy in Missouri, and how Missouri providers apply the SAFE Act's carve-out for patients already in treatment when the patient is not a state resident, is not sourced.

Whether Missouri has any state-level restriction on identity documents, driver's licence or birth-certificate markers is not addressed in this inventory; the document rules described here are federal.
